smm_pool.title: Meta Adds Automatic Customer Exclusions
smm_pool.text: Meta is making a change to Customer Lifecycle Strategy that has the potential to make the feature infinitely more useful. While I do think it could use some additional tweaks, it’s a great step in the right direction. If you’re not familiar with Customer Lifecycle Strategy, it’s the new dropdown menu at the top of ad sets that allows advertisers to make a selection between two audience pools: Get conversions from all audiences Acquire new customers Meta is nudging advertisers away from custom audience exclusions within the main Audience section of the ad set to Customer Lifecycle Strategy when the goal is new customer acquisition. But much about the original version of this feature was flawed. Advertisers seemed to believe it had magical powers when “Acquire new customers” was selected. It does not . You still need to manually select custom audiences to exclude. And while Meta can attempt to select audiences for you automatically, the logic behind this selection is often hilariously wrong. But this latest update makes Customer Lifecycle Strategy far more useful. Automatic Customer Exclusions Now when I select the option to acquire new customers, I notice something new under the section to exclude existing customers: “ Automatically created: Customers from your conversion data (730 days).” When expanded, it looks like this… To help you reach new customers, Meta will automatically exclude existing ones based on your ad account’s conversion data. In other words, Meta is no longer relying on your defined custom audiences to exclude your existing customers. Instead, it’s the people who have fired the “purchase” conversion event. By default, the retention window is 730 days (two years), which is the relatively new maximum available for purchase events . But you have five options: 730 days 180 days 90 days 60 days 30 days This way, you can automatically exclude people who have purchased from you without providing a custom audience. This is helpful because the accuracy and completeness of a custom audience can be undercut by advertiser error. Remember: Meta Has the Data An option like this reinforces a point that I’ve attempted to drill home for several years now: Meta doesn’t need us to define who is important to our business with custom audiences because that data is already known. smm_pool.title: Which CTA Button Should You Use?
smm_pool.text: Advertisers have long flown blind on CTA buttons. It makes sense that “Learn More” might drive more clicks while “Shop Now” would drive more intent. But it’s also never been clear how much these CTA buttons matter. Finally, we might have some helpful information. You may have seen the following message recently when creating an ad in Ads Manager: ‘See details’ is the default call to action text. ‘See details’ drives up to 2.3% higher CVR compared to ‘Learn more.’ What does this mean for advertisers’ use of CTA buttons? What it Means While a difference in performance between CTA buttons makes sense intuitively, I’ve long questioned whether that difference is significant or predictable. And this message from Meta makes that especially questionable. Meta’s highlighting that “See details” drives up to a 2.3% higher conversion rate than “Learn More”? UP TO 2.3%. It tells me that the difference is negligible and not worth obsessing over. Don’t worry about split testing CTA buttons unless you have the budget that could highlight meaningful differences. Any variances are likely to fall within a range of randomness. What About Other CTA Buttons? It’s interesting that Meta believes the difference in performance is enough to make “See details” the new default. I only wish that Meta would share data on all of the CTA buttons to give us more to work with. They have the data on “Shop Now,” “Sign Up,” and more. Why not share it? smm_pool.text: What is an employee advocacy program? An employee advocacy program is a structured initiative that encourages employees to share company-approved content on their personal social media accounts to extend brand reach and build trust. It’s a powerful part of any social media marketing and content strategy . Instead of relying only on your brand’s accounts to do the talking, employees post about your company on platforms like LinkedIn, X, or wherever they’re already active. Sometimes that content is promotional, like a new campaign, product launch, or company milestone. Other times it’s cultural, offering a peek into what it’s actually like to work at your company. The reason it works is simple: people trust other people more than they trust corporations. In fact, 88% of consumers say trusting a brand is an important or critical purchase criterion, on par with quality and value, according to Edelman. When your employees share authentic stories, it humanizes your brand, boosts your organic reach, and helps you connect with your target audience in ways standard corporate messaging just can’t. In short, every employee share strengthens both your internal company culture and your external trust, turning your team into your most credible marketing channel . An effective analytics strategy starts with clear goals, a unified tool, and a consistent reporting cadence that connects social performance to business outcomes. What is social media analytics? Social media analytics means the collection, analysis, and reporting of data points that help you measure the performance of your social media accounts and guide business decisions. These are the KPIs and metrics that help you assess and refine your social media marketing strategy on both macro and micro levels. That includes data from your own content (owned), conversations about your brand (earned), and your ad campaigns (paid). For enterprise teams, analytics goes beyond what’s available in native platform dashboards. It often means integrating social media data with web analytics, CRM systems, and business intelligence tools to get a unified view of performance across brands, regions, and channels. At a conceptual level, there are four analytical approaches that apply to social media data: Descriptive: What happened? (e.g., engagement dropped 12% last month) Diagnostic: Why did it happen? (e.g., posting frequency decreased during a team transition) Predictive: What’s likely to happen next? (e.g., engagement will rebound if posting cadence returns to normal) Prescriptive: What should we do about it?
